title: Walrus operator should not make code confusing
description: The walrus operator (:=) introduced in Python 3.8 allows assignment expressions within larger expressions. While this can make code more concise, it can also make code harder to read and understand when used inappropriately. This rule flags confusing uses of the walrus operator that decrease code clarity.
message: This walrus operator usage makes the code confusing. Consider using a regular assignment statement instead.
impact: Confusing walrus operator usage can make code harder to read, debug, and maintain, leading to increased development time and potential bugs.
recommendation: Use the walrus operator sparingly and only when it genuinely improves code readability. Prefer regular assignment statements when the assignment doesn't need to be part of a larger expression.

compliant.description: Simple condition capture in if statement

compliant.code:
# Good: Avoids recomputing expensive function
results = [y for x in data if (y := expensive_func(x)) > threshold]

# Good: Clear intent with regular assignment
result = compute_value()
if result > 10:
    process(result)

noncompliant.description: Walrus operator in complex nested expression
Walrus operator with side effects in unexpected places
noncompliant.code:
# Bad: Assignment buried in function argument
process_data(items, threshold=(limit := calculate_limit()))
print(f"Used limit: {limit}")

# Bad: Unclear precedence and flow
result = (x := get_value()) + (y := x * 2) if x > 0 else (z := default_value())

noncompliant.description: Walrus operator where regular assignment is clearer
noncompliant.code:
# Bad: Walrus doesn't add value here
print(f"Processing {name := user.get_name()}")
# The name is only used once, regular assignment would be clearer

# Bad: Multiple nested assignments are confusing
data = [(x := item.value, y := x * 2, z := y + (w := offset)) for item in items]

why_is_this_an_issue: The walrus operator (:=) can significantly improve code conciseness in specific scenarios, but when overused or used inappropriately, it can make code much harder to read and understand. Complex expressions with multiple walrus operators, assignments in unexpected locations, or cases where regular assignment statements would be clearer all contribute to reduced code maintainability. The operator should enhance readability, not hinder it.
how_to_fix: 1. Replace confusing walrus operators with regular assignment statements when the expression doesn't benefit from inline assignment. 2. Limit the use of walrus operators to cases where they genuinely improve readability, such as eliminating loop-and-a-half patterns or avoiding duplicate expensive computations. 3. Avoid nesting multiple walrus operators in the same expression. 4. Don't use walrus operators just to make code shorter if it makes it less clear. 5. Consider the cognitive load on future readers of the code.
